# A finite-cap cut-and-fill theorem for strictly convex bodies

This is an actual ordinary convex-body variation in every d>=2. It
preserves volume and all but one of a finite collection of cap volumes
and central section measures, while strictly decreasing the remaining
cap volume and increasing its section measure. It supplies a local
structural restriction on constrained extremizers. It does not prove
a polytope reduction, a simplex reduction, or a mixed-integer theorem.

## Theorem

Let d>=2 and let K be a strictly convex body in R^d with 0 in int K.
Let u_1,...,u_N be nonzero normals whose UNORIENTED hyperplanes

    Pi_j={x:u_j.x=0}

are pairwise distinct. For each j define

    q_j(K)=vol_d(K intersect {u_j.x>=0}),
    sigma_j(K)=H_(d-1)(K intersect Pi_j)/||u_j||.

All sigma_j are positive and finite. Fix any index i. There are convex
bodies K_epsilon, for all sufficiently small epsilon>0, such that
0 remains in their interior, K_epsilon tends to K in Hausdorff distance,
and

    vol_d(K_epsilon)=vol_d(K),
    q_j(K_epsilon)=q_j(K)                 for j!=i,
    q_i(K_epsilon)<q_i(K),
    sigma_j(K_epsilon)=sigma_j(K)         for j!=i,
    sigma_i(K_epsilon)>sigma_i(K).                               (1)

If N>=2 and

    lambda_j(K)=(1/sigma_j(K))/sum_l(1/sigma_l(K)),

then lambda_i(K_epsilon)<lambda_i(K), while all other lambda_j
increase. If i is initially an index of the smallest lambda, the
smallest normalized inverse-section weight strictly decreases.

The normals, source, and halfspaces stay fixed throughout. In
particular every upper constraint coordinatewise nondecreasing in
(q_1,...,q_N), with total volume fixed, remains feasible. This includes
the ordinary three-cap profile used in the planar investigation.

## 1. A source-section endpoint away from all the other planes

Because the planes are distinct, Pi_i intersect Pi_j is a proper
linear subspace of Pi_i for every j!=i. Finitely many proper linear
subspaces do not cover Pi_i. One elementary proof is to take the
product of nonzero linear functionals vanishing on those subspaces:
it is a nonzero polynomial on Pi_i, so it is nonzero at some vector.
Choose such a nonzero vector w in Pi_i. On its positive ray let P be
the boundary point of K. Then

    P in Pi_i intersect boundary K,
    P notin Pi_j for j!=i.

Existence and uniqueness along the ray follow from compact convexity
and 0 in int K. Set P_epsilon=(1+epsilon)P; it is outside K and remains
in Pi_i. Let

    L_epsilon=conv(K union {P_epsilon}).

Define J={j!=i:u_j.P>0}. In a sufficiently small neighborhood O of P,
the signs for all j!=i stay fixed: positive for J, negative otherwise.

## 2. Strict convexity localizes the ENTIRE added region

For every open neighborhood O of P,

    L_epsilon\K subset O for all sufficiently small epsilon.      (2)

Suppose not. Choose epsilon_m tending to zero and points x_m in
(L_epsilon_m\K)\O. Their boundedness and compactness give a subsequence
tending to x outside O. For each m, strict separation supplies a unit
normal n_m with n_m.x_m>h_K(n_m). A subsequence tends to a unit n.
Since the support function of L_epsilon is
max(h_K(n),n.P_epsilon), the separating inequality forces
n_m.P_epsilon_m>h_K(n_m). In the limit n.P>=h_K(n), and equality holds
since P belongs to K. Also

    L_epsilon subset K+epsilon||P|| B_2,

so x belongs to K. Passing to the limit in the separating inequalities
gives n.x>=h_K(n), and again equality holds. Thus both x and P belong
to one exposed face of K. Strict convexity makes every exposed face
a singleton, so x=P, a contradiction. This proves (2).

Let D_+ and D_- be the volumes of the added region on the positive
and negative sides of Pi_i. Both are strictly positive. To see this,
take a fixed small ball centered at 0 inside K. The convex hull of
that ball with P_epsilon has positive-volume cones approaching
P_epsilon from both sides of Pi_i. A sufficiently small ball about
the exterior point P_epsilon is disjoint from K; its intersections
with both cones have positive volume. Put D=D_++D_->0. The added
region's intersection with Pi_i is d-volume null.

Moreover D tends to zero, because the displayed outer-parallel-set
containment and continuity from above of finite Lebesgue measure give
vol_d(L_epsilon) tending to vol_d(K).

By (2), every added point has signature J or J union {i}. The fill
therefore changes cap volumes by D on indices in J, by D_+ at i,
and by zero on every other index.

## 3. A fixed exposed cap with the complementary signature

There is a boundary point R, arbitrarily close to P, for which

    u_i.R>0,
    u_j.R has the same sign as u_j.P for every j!=i.               (3)

Indeed choose vectors w_delta tending to P with u_i.w_delta>0,
and take their radial boundary points. The radial map is continuous
because a convex body containing a ball about 0 has a continuous
Minkowski gauge. For an elementary justification, the gauge is
subadditive and is bounded above by ||x||/rho when B(0,rho) subset K;
applying subadditivity in both orders makes it Lipschitz. The radial
boundary map is x divided by its positive gauge near nonzero P.
Thus these boundary points tend to P, proving (3).

Fix one such R distinct from P. Let ell be any supporting functional
at R and put h=h_K(ell). Strict convexity means its support face is
exactly {R}; consequently ell.P<h. Also h>0 because 0 is interior.

The shallow caps

    E_eta=K intersect {ell.x>=h-eta}

shrink to R as eta decreases to zero. Otherwise compactness of points
outside a neighborhood of R would give a second point of the same
support face. Choose eta_0>0 so that E_eta0 lies strictly inside every
open halfspace specified by (3), and is also disjoint from a fixed
neighborhood of P. Its volume is positive because every proper cut
of a convex body with interior has positive cap volume.

For all sufficiently small epsilon, (2) makes the added region disjoint
from E_eta0 and its containing cap halfspace. More explicitly choose
the neighborhood O in (2) to lie in {ell.x<h-eta0}; then

    L_epsilon intersect {ell.x>=h-eta}=E_eta
    for 0<=eta<=eta0.                                           (4)

The cap volumes of E_eta are continuous, strictly increasing from zero
for 0<eta<=eta0. Continuity follows from null hyperplane sections and
dominated convergence; strict increase follows from positive volume
of the interior slab between two proper thresholds. Since D tends to
zero, choose the unique eta=eta(epsilon) with vol_d(E_eta)=D. It tends
to zero. Define the ACTUAL final body

    K_epsilon=L_epsilon intersect {ell.x<=h-eta(epsilon)}.         (5)

The removed cap has exactly signature J union {i}, up to its null
boundary. Therefore it cancels the fill's D in every index of J,
removes D from index i, and changes no other cap. Its net change at
i is D_+-D=-D_-<0. It also restores the original total volume.
This proves all cap-volume assertions in (1).

## 4. Exact sections, the source, and Hausdorff convergence

For j!=i the added region misses Pi_j by (2), and the shaved cap misses
every Pi_j by its strict signature. Hence those central sections
remain exactly the same sets. On the selected plane,

    L_epsilon intersect Pi_i
      =conv((K intersect Pi_i) union {P_epsilon}).                 (6)

Every point of the hull is a convex combination of P_epsilon and one
point of K. Since P_epsilon is in Pi_i, a combination in Pi_i must use
a point of K in Pi_i (or just P_epsilon). This proves (6). The body
K intersect Pi_i has dimension d-1 and contains a relative ball about
0. The point P_epsilon is outside it. Its convex hull with an exterior
point therefore has strictly larger (d-1)-volume: a separating plane
in Pi_i, together with an interior relative ball, gives a cone of
positive (d-1)-volume outside the original section. This works also
when d-1=1, where it is an interval extension. The shave does not meet
Pi_i. Thus all section assertions in (1) follow.

A fixed sufficiently small ball about 0 is untouched by the localized
shave, and L_epsilon contains K, so 0 remains interior. Finally

    (1-eta(epsilon)/h)K subset K_epsilon
        subset K+epsilon||P||B_2                               (7)

for sufficiently small epsilon. The first inclusion uses convexity,
0 in K, and ell.x<=h on K; the second follows from the filled hull.
Both outer bounds tend to K, proving Hausdorff convergence without
an exchange of selected points or an unproved minimizing sequence.

For N>=2, the normalized inverse-weight assertions follow from
lambda_i=x/(x+C), with x=1/sigma_i strictly decreasing and
C=sum_(j!=i)1/sigma_j fixed and positive. The other normalized weights
increase because their numerators stay fixed and their denominator
decreases.

## 5. Scope and consequences

The theorem gives an actual admissible local direction at every
strictly convex K in a feasible fixed-volume, cap-upper-bound class.
Thus no such K can locally minimize a specified normalized inverse
section weight over the full class of convex bodies when N>=2.
The new bodies need not be strictly convex.

Distinct UNORIENTED cutting planes matter. If both opposite caps on
the same plane were included, fixing total volume while decreasing
one would necessarily increase the other. Nor does the section
increase make sense in d=1: its central H_0 section is fixed. Those
cases are deliberately excluded, not silently discarded.

The locality proof can fail at a flat exposed face through P. A new
hull region may then run along that entire face and cross other
cutting planes. The theorem therefore supplies no all-polytope
reduction or termination procedure. It is also an ordinary-body
deformation only: preserving compatibility with additional fibers
would require further hypotheses and is not claimed.

## 6. Extension to a localized contact star, without strict convexity

Here K is an arbitrary convex body with 0 in its interior. Keep the
distinct planes and d>=2, and choose any

    P in boundary K intersect Pi_i,
    P notin Pi_j for j!=i.

Define its ENTIRE contact star

    E(P)=union {F(K,n): ||n||=1, n.P=h_K(n)},
    F(K,n)={x in K:n.x=h_K(n)}.                                  (8)

This union includes all exposed faces whose supporting hyperplane
contains P. It is compact: the defining pairs (n,x) form a closed
subset of the compact set S^(d-1) x K, and E(P) is its projection.
It is not sufficient to select just one favorable face through P.

Assume the precise locality condition

    E(P) intersect Pi_j is empty for every j!=i.                  (9)

Then ALL conclusions (1) hold, using this P, even though K need not
be strictly convex.

First, the separating-normal proof of Section 2 now shows that the
entire added region L_epsilon\K localizes to E(P): any limit of
points of that region lies in some exposed face containing P, which
is exactly (8). Every face in (8) is convex and contains P. Under
(9), each u_j, j!=i, has the same strict sign on that entire face as
at P. Thus the whole compact E(P) has these signs, with a uniform
positive separation from the other planes. Its sufficiently small
neighborhood U consequently has one constant signature J on all
indices other than i. The fill has only signatures J and J union {i},
and positive volume on both sides of Pi_i as before.

It remains to construct a removable cap with signature J union {i}
without declaring a point in the interior of a flat face to be exposed.
The following normal-cone argument does so. Put

    N_K(P)={n:n.(x-P)<=0 for every x in K}.

This is a closed convex cone with a nonzero element n. Neither u_i
nor -u_i belongs to it: u_i.P=0 while h_K(u_i)>0 and h_K(-u_i)>0.
In particular n is not parallel to u_i. The ray n+t u_i, t>=0,
leaves N_K(P) at a finite last parameter t_*. Otherwise divide an
unbounded sequence of its cone elements by t to infer u_i in N_K(P).
Convexity and closedness make its parameter set the closed interval
[0,t_*]. Let n_*=n+t_*u_i, which is nonzero since n is not parallel
to u_i. Then n_* is a support normal at P, but

    ell_delta=n_*+delta u_i notin N_K(P) for every delta>0.

Consequently h_K(ell_delta)>ell_delta.P=n_*.P. Every x in the exposed
face F(K,ell_delta) obeys n_*.x<=n_*.P, so

    delta u_i.x=h_K(ell_delta)-n_*.x>0.                           (10)

As delta decreases to zero, all these maximizing faces localize to
F(K,n_*) subset E(P), by compactness and continuity of support
functions. Choose and FIX one sufficiently small delta>0. Its whole
exposed face G=F(K,ell_delta) then lies in U and, by (10), strictly
on the positive side of Pi_i. Compactness gives strict separation
from all the cutting planes. No uniqueness of G is asserted or needed.

Write ell=ell_delta and h=h_K(ell)>0. Shallow ell-caps of K localize
to G. Choose eta_0>0 such that

    K intersect {ell.x>=h-eta_0}

is compactly contained in the signature region J union {i}, and
eta_0<min(h/2,h-ell.P). For sufficiently small epsilon, ell.P_epsilon
is below h-eta_0, so h_(L_epsilon)(ell)=h. The corresponding cap of
L_epsilon is also contained in the same open signature region. Indeed
otherwise a convergent sequence of contrary cap points, using
L_epsilon tending to K in Hausdorff distance, would limit to a point
of the displayed closed K cap outside that open region.

Thus the L_epsilon cap-area function from threshold h down to
h-eta_0 is continuous, starts at zero, and reaches at least the fixed
positive K cap volume. It has a cap of exact area D, the total added
volume. Shave that ACTUAL cap. It may contain newly added points;
this does not affect the signature accounting. Its volume D cancels
every J-index gain, and decreases the i-th cap by exactly D_-.

Its depth eta(epsilon) tends to zero: at every fixed positive depth
the L_epsilon cap contains a K cap of fixed positive volume, whereas
D tends to zero. Hence the contraction containment (7) again proves
Hausdorff convergence and preservation of an interior source ball.
The cap misses all central planes, so the exact section argument (6)
also remains valid. This completes the extension.

## 7. A necessary flat-face incidence at a constrained local minimum

Consider a local minimum of a specified lambda_i in a fixed-volume
class defined by upper constraints coordinatewise nondecreasing in the
listed cap masses, with 0 kept interior and N>=2. The preceding
construction proves the following necessary condition: for EVERY
P in boundary K intersect Pi_i that avoids all other cutting planes,
there must be some j!=i and an exposed face F containing P with

    F intersect Pi_j nonempty.                                  (11)

Otherwise (9) would hold and the actual nearby feasible body would
strictly lower lambda_i. Because P is not in Pi_j, this face is
nontrivial. This is a local structural restriction; no existence of
the local minimum is presumed.

In the planar three-line problem the two endpoints of the selected
central chord automatically avoid the other lines: distinct lines
through 0 intersect only at 0, while 0 is interior. Thus EACH endpoint
must lie on a flat exposed segment that reaches another cut line, at
a nonzero point on one of its rays. The analogous conclusion holds
for a local minimum of the smallest inverse weight when i is an
index attaining that minimum.

This leaves faces meeting multiple cut rays as a real exceptional
configuration. It does not turn the body into a triangle or establish
a finite sequence of reducing operations.

## 8. Why one favorable face is insufficient: an exact planar example

Let K=conv{P,R,S}, where P=(0,1), R=(1,1), S=(-1,-2), and use the
three planar normals (1,0),(0,1),(-1,-1). The origin is the centroid
and is interior. The upper endpoint of K intersect {x=0} is P.
Its exposed edge P R is contained in {y>0,x+y>0}, exactly the favorable
two-sector neighborhood for the first plane. But its OTHER exposed
edge P S crosses both y=0 and x+y=0.

For P_epsilon=(0,1+epsilon), the filled hull is conv{P_epsilon,R,S}.
Direct edge intersections show that the normalized second section
increases by

    2epsilon/[3(3+epsilon)],

and the normalized third section increases by

    3epsilon/[4(4+epsilon)].

For example, the second section has endpoints 1/3 and
-(1+epsilon)/(3+epsilon), while the third has coordinate endpoints
1/5 and -(1+epsilon)/(4+epsilon). Their original lengths are 2/3
and 9/20, respectively. Both changes are strictly positive.
Thus selecting the favorable face P R alone does not give a
one-section deformation. Its full contact star also contains P S,
which fails (9), exactly as required by the theorem.
